findings.snippet: a tombstone in Egypt is dated Ramadan 29 AH
findings.problem: The tombstone of 'Urwa b. Thabit dated Ramadan 29 AH (650 CE) is reported from Cyprus, not Egypt. The earliest dated Egyptian tombstone is a different one (Aswan, 31 AH).
findings.correction: a tombstone in Cyprus is dated Ramadan 29 AH
sources: https://www.islamic-awareness.org/history/islam/inscriptions/urwa (An Arabic Inscription From Cyprus, 29 AH / 650 CE; Elad)

findings.snippet: show the same surah text in the first Islamic century
findings.problem: The Sana'a palimpsest lower text contains many variants from the standard Uthmanic text (Sadeghi and Bergmann, Arabica 57, 2010), and the Birmingham folios are only a small portion. Saying they show "the same text" overstates it.
findings.correction: show a text that is, in the portions preserved, very close to today's Quran. The Sana'a lower text does contain variants, which scholars debate
sources: Sadeghi & Bergmann, "The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qur'an of the Prophet", Arabica 57 (2010) 343-436

findings.snippet: Zayd ibn Thabit accepted a passage only if it was found in writing and confirmed by memorisers (Bukhari 4986)
findings.problem: Bukhari 4986 narrates the collection and the finding of the last verses of al-Tawba with Abu Khuzayma. The two-witness (written plus memorised) rule is from later sources such as Ibn Abi Dawud and Ibn Hajar (Fath al-Bari 8/437), not stated in this hadith.
findings.correction: Zayd collected the Quran from written fragments and from memorisers (Bukhari 4986); later scholars such as Ibn Hajar explain that he required two witnesses for each verse

findings.snippet: Not one Companion accused Uthman of changing the Quran, even though some of them later fought against him politically.
findings.problem: Ibn Mas'ud objected strongly to the burning of his codex and to Zayd being preferred (reported in Bukhari 4987-4988 context and Ibn Abi Dawud, Masahif). He did not accuse Uthman of changing a verse, but "not one Companion objected" is too strong.
findings.correction: No Companion is reported to have accused Uthman of adding or removing a verse, although Ibn Mas'ud objected to the burning of his own codex and to the choice of Zayd

findings.snippet: No other ancient scripture has both an unbroken oral chain and dated manuscripts from the generation of its founder.
findings.problem: Universal claim that cannot be verified (Vedic oral tradition, Avesta and other scriptures have oral chains). The Birmingham folios are dated by radiocarbon of the parchment, with a range up to 645 CE, which does not itself date the text as an Uthmanic text.
findings.correction: Few ancient scriptures combine a continuous oral recitation tradition with manuscripts radiocarbon-dated to within decades of the founder.
sources: Radiocarbon dating of Birmingham Mingana 1572a/Parisino-Petropolitanus: 568-645 CE (95.4%)

findings.snippet: Seyfeddin Kara ( The Integrity of the Qur'an ) concludes the codex can be dated with certainty to before Umar's death (23/644).
findings.problem: Could not open the book (Edinburgh University Press, open access) to confirm the wording. Kara uses isnad-cum-matn analysis of hadith to argue for early codification; "with certainty" looks stronger than a hadith-based dating can claim.
findings.correction: Seyfeddin Kara (The Integrity of the Qur'an) argues from isnad-cum-matn analysis that the codification dates to the earliest period, before Uthman.

findings.snippet: notes that newly found fragments support an early fixed text and that the "revisionist" theories of a late, evolving Quran have failed
findings.problem: Neuwirth (Cambridge Companion, 2006, ch. "Structural, linguistic and literary features") does not, as far as could be confirmed, say this. Neuwirth sees the Quran as a text that grew within the Prophet's community over his lifetime and is itself critical of the traditional account. Quote not found.
findings.correction: Angelika Neuwirth, in the Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an, treats the Quran as a text that took shape in the Prophet's own community, and rejects late-dating theories such as Wansbrough's (verify wording and page before quoting)
sources: Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an (2006), ed. McAuliffe

findings.snippet: "There is probably no other book in the world which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
findings.problem: Muir's words (Life of Mahomet, introduction) are "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text." Word order is altered in a quotation. Muir also held that this purity referred to the Uthmanic text and that Muhammad was not the sole source.
findings.correction: "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
sources: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (1858-61), introductory chapters

findings.snippet: Andrew Rippin , Neal Robinson , H.A.R. Gibb , R.V.C. Bodley , C.C. Torrey , Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri all make similar statements.
findings.problem: Rippin is a leading sceptic of early Quran history and does not say the text is unaltered. Torrey argued the Quran was fixed by Muhammad himself but had other views on Muhammad's sources. A blanket "all make similar statements" is not supported.
findings.correction: Neal Robinson, H.A.R. Gibb, R.V.C. Bodley, C.C. Torrey, Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri make similar statements (check each citation before quoting; Rippin should be removed).
sources: Rippin, The Qur'an and its Interpretative Tradition; Companion to the Qur'an (Blackwell)

findings.snippet: Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, now treat an early fixed text as the starting point.
findings.problem: Neuwirth and Sinai accept that the Quran largely goes back to Muhammad's time, but both describe a text that developed (Neuwirth: community-shaped, multi-stage; Sinai: some post-Muhammadan editing). Neither says the text is "unaltered".
findings.correction: Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, accept that most of the Quran goes back to Muhammad's lifetime, while still describing a text that developed within his community.
sources: Sinai, The Qur'an: A Historical-Critical Introduction (2017)

findings.snippet: scholars who have no stake in defending Islam agree the Quran has not been altered
findings.problem: Overreach: the cited scholars concede early origin and reliability of the consonantal text, not unanimous agreement that nothing changed. Several (Sinai, Neuwirth, Rippin) describe editing or development.
findings.correction: scholars who have no stake in defending Islam increasingly accept that the Quran text goes back to Muhammad's generation

findings.snippet: Ibn Mujahid's survey found that only about 700 of the Quran's roughly 77,000 words differ between the readings
findings.problem: No source found for Ibn Mujahid counting 700 differing words; his Kitab al-Sab'a lists the seven readers and their differences but not this total. The 1% figure is circulated without citation.
findings.correction: Ibn Mujahid's Kitab al-Sab'a records that the differences between the canonical readings affect a small fraction of the Quran's words, mostly vowels and verb forms.
sources: Ibn Mujahid, Kitab al-Sab'a fi al-Qira'at

findings.snippet: Each canonical reading needs a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) chain to the Prophet
findings.problem: Ibn al-Jazari's widely used criteria require a sound (sahih) chain, agreement with the Uthmanic outline and Arabic grammar. Mutawatir is the stricter condition held by some scholars (e.g. al-Suyuti discusses both). Stated as settled when it is disputed.
findings.correction: Each canonical reading needs a sound chain to the Prophet (many scholars require mass transmission), must fit the Uthmanic consonantal outline, and must be correct Arabic.
sources: Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr

findings.snippet: both taught by the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 2419)
findings.problem: The seven ahruf of Bukhari 2419 and the canonical qira'at are not the same thing in classical scholarship; the exact relation between ahruf and the ten readings is disputed (some say ahruf are not the qira'at at all).
findings.correction: The Prophet approved different recitations (the seven ahruf), and the canonical qira'at are held by scholars to preserve authorised recitations; how exactly the ahruf relate to the qira'at is discussed among scholars.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2419; Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Tafsir intro on the seven ahruf

findings.snippet: graded weak by al-Arna'ut
findings.problem: Ibn Majah 1944 is graded hasan by al-Albani and the sheep detail is criticised by others. The specific grading by al-Arna'ut could not be confirmed. The claim that only Ibn Ishaq narrates the sheep is made by critics of the report.
findings.correction: (graded hasan by al-Albani; some scholars regard the sheep detail as weak because it comes only through Ibn Ishaq)

findings.snippet: "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold…" Ibn Abbas said he did not know whether it was from the Quran. Ubayy said they thought it was until Surah al-Takathur was revealed (Bukhari 6440)
findings.problem: On sunnah.com, Bukhari 6437 is the Ibn Abbas narration, 6438 has Ubayy's statement and 6440 is Anas. Citing only 6440 is imprecise.

findings.snippet: Ibn Mas'ud called al-Fatiha "the seven oft-repeated" and urged reciting the two Mu'awwidhatayn.
findings.problem: Reports that Ibn Mas'ud did not write the Mu'awwidhatayn in his codex are in Musnad Ahmad and Bukhari 4977 (Ubayy's report) and graded sound; saying he "urged" reciting them needs a cited source. The paragraph handles this with "At most, he did not write", but the first sentence should not imply there is no report.
findings.correction: Ibn Mas'ud is reported not to have written the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his personal codex (Musnad Ahmad; see Bukhari 4977), and scholars explain this as his view that they were protective prayers or that they needed no writing.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4977; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari 8/741

findings.snippet: Ubayy himself dictated to Zayd during Uthman's compilation (Kanz al-'Ummal 4789)
findings.problem: Could not verify the Kanz al-Ummal number 4789. The report that Ubayy dictated is in Ibn Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Masahif and cited elsewhere.
findings.correction: Ubayy is reported to have dictated to Zayd during Uthman's compilation (Ibn Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Masahif)

findings.snippet: The reports in Musnad Ahmad run through Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad and 'Asim, whose memory was criticised
findings.problem: Musnad Ahmad's narration on al-Ahzab's length (from Ubayy) runs through Zirr and 'Asim ibn Bahdala; Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad is on a different narration. Could not confirm both are in the same chain.
findings.correction: The reports in Musnad Ahmad run through 'Asim ibn Bahdala, whose memory was criticised, and through other chains with their own weaknesses

findings.snippet: Before that, no one in the world, Muslim, Jewish or Christian, could read an Egyptian royal title or funerary text.
findings.problem: Medieval Arabic writers such as Ibn Wahshiyya (Shawq al-Mustaham, 10th century) and Dhul-Nun al-Misri claimed to decipher hieroglyphs, and Coptic speakers retained some knowledge. Their decipherments were largely wrong, but "no one could read" the language is too strong.
findings.correction: Before 1822, nobody could correctly read Egyptian royal titles or funerary texts, although medieval Arabic authors such as Ibn Wahshiyya attempted to decipher hieroglyphs.
sources: Okasha El Daly, Egyptology: The Missing Millennium (2005)

findings.snippet: On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus, the creator-claim of Pharaoh) the Bible actually says the opposite.
findings.problem: The Bible does not give a creator-claim of Pharaoh in the Moses story (Ezek 29:3 is a later prophetic oracle). Also, many scholars regard the Hyksos/Joseph identification and the Exodus date as uncertain, so "confirmed by archaeology" is overstated.
findings.correction: On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus), the Bible differs from the Quran.

findings.snippet: Every detail below was confirmed only after those decipherments.
findings.problem: Several of the details listed are not archaeologically confirmed (Joseph's date under the Hyksos, Moses' Ramesside date) and some, such as fired brick, have earlier Egyptian attestation. This is stated as settled.
findings.correction: Several details below have been argued to fit evidence uncovered after those decipherments.

findings.snippet: This matches Egyptian history exactly, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" anachronistically for both.
findings.problem: Whether the Bible's "Pharaoh" in Genesis is anachronistic is disputed (K. Kitchen argues the title was already used by the narrator's time), and linking Joseph to the Hyksos is a hypothesis. "Exactly" overstates it.
findings.correction: This fits the Egyptian use of "pharaoh" as a royal title from the New Kingdom, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler. (Many Egyptologists call the biblical usage retrospective.)
sources: Shaw & Nicholson, British Museum Dictionary of Ancient Egypt
K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003)

findings.snippet: Joseph lived well before that, plausibly under the Hyksos
findings.problem: The historicity and date of Joseph are not established; the Hyksos placement is one conjecture among several (Middle Kingdom, Hyksos, Amarna).
findings.correction: Joseph is placed by some scholars well before the New Kingdom, plausibly under the Hyksos, but his date is uncertain.

findings.snippet: Alan Gardiner ( Egyptian Grammar , p.75) and W.V. Davies ( Egyptian Hieroglyphs , p.45) give the same dating.
findings.problem: Page numbers could not be checked against the editions. Gardiner's Egyptian Grammar discusses per-aa under the sign for house, in the 3rd edition near p.75, but the exact claim ("from the New Kingdom, especially Thutmose III") should be checked.
findings.correction: Alan Gardiner (Egyptian Grammar) and W.V. Davies (Egyptian Hieroglyphs) give a similar dating (check edition and page).

findings.snippet: it calls Moses' ruler Pharaoh 74 times
findings.problem: The commonly cited count is 74 but depends on how verses are counted; varies by source (about 73-74).
findings.correction: it calls Moses' ruler Pharaoh dozens of times (about 74)

findings.snippet: Baked brick was rare in Egypt and appears in the Ramesside period, which is Moses' era.
findings.problem: Fired brick is attested in Egypt before the Ramesside period: in Middle Kingdom Nubian fortresses (Buhen etc.) and in the New Kingdom at Thebes. Petrie's Nebesheh and Defenneh evidence is one example, not the first appearance. The Ramesside date of Moses is also only one of several proposals (an earlier date is argued by others).
findings.correction: Baked brick was rare in Egypt, though it is attested in Middle Kingdom Nubian forts and in New Kingdom Thebes, and Petrie found Ramesside examples at Nebesheh. Many place Moses in the Ramesside era, but this is debated.
sources: Spencer, Brick Architecture in Ancient Egypt (1979)

findings.snippet: in the one era where Egyptology finds it
findings.problem: Egyptology also finds fired brick in the Middle Kingdom (Nubia) and the New Kingdom (Thebes).
findings.correction: in an era where Egyptology finds it
sources: Spencer, Brick Architecture in Ancient Egypt (1979)

findings.snippet: Petrie's excavations found fired brick introduced in Ramesside times in the Delta, in a tomb bearing a cartouche of Ramesses II.
findings.problem: Petrie (Tanis II, 1888) reports burnt brick at Nebesheh and Defenneh in the Delta in the Ramesside era; the "introduced" wording is the argument's, not Petrie's. Could not open the Heidelberg scan to confirm the cartouche detail.
findings.correction: Petrie found burnt brick in the Ramesside Delta (Nebesheh) in a tomb bearing Ramesside names.
sources: Petrie, Tanis Part II: Nebesheh and Defenneh (1888)

findings.snippet: In Abraham's Mesopotamia (early 2nd millennium BCE), the leading cosmic gods were Ishtar (Venus), Sin (the moon) and Shamash (the sun), shown together on kudurru boundary stones and seals.
findings.problem: Kudurru boundary stones are Kassite (c. 1500-1100 BCE), several centuries after the early 2nd millennium BCE date given for Abraham. The Sin, Shamash, Ishtar triad is attested earlier on seals, but the kudurru evidence is later. The order and identification of the Quranic "star" as Venus is a tafsir opinion.
findings.correction: In Mesopotamia from the 3rd millennium onward the Moon-god Sin, Sun-god Shamash and Ishtar (Venus) were prominent, and they appear together on seals and on Kassite kudurru stones (later 2nd millennium BCE).
sources: Pizzimenti, The Astral Family in Kassite Kudurrus Reliefs

findings.snippet: The Quran reflects the actual religion of Abraham's world, which was rediscovered only by modern Assyriology.
findings.problem: The Quran does not name Ishtar, Sin or Shamash, and Abraham's historicity and date are not established by archaeology. "Rediscovered only by modern Assyriology" overlooks that Greek/Jewish/Muslim writers already knew Mesopotamian astral worship (e.g. Sabians of Harran, Ibn Kathir).
findings.correction: The Quran's sequence star, moon, sun is consistent with the astral worship of Mesopotamia and Harran.

findings.snippet: Ibn Kathir already explained the kawkab as Venus
findings.problem: Could not confirm Ibn Kathir's wording on 6:76; al-Tabari and others list opinions (e.g. Zuhra/Venus, Jupiter), and Ibn Kathir reports differing views.
findings.correction: Some early commentators, including those recorded by Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, said the kawkab was Venus (al-Zuhra)

findings.snippet: Dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC is "sustainable"
findings.problem: Scholars of the Bible and Near East (e.g. Finkelstein, Van Seters) doubt Abraham's historicity; "sustainable" is a conservative evangelical position, not a consensus.
findings.correction: Some scholars regard dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC as sustainable, though many scholars doubt he is a historical figure.

findings.snippet: fire, water and earth (Apocalypse of Abraham 7)
findings.problem: The Apocalypse of Abraham ch. 7 reasons through fire, water, earth, sun and moon in turn, so the list is incomplete; verify against a translation.
findings.correction: fire, water, earth, sun and moon (Apocalypse of Abraham 7)

findings.snippet: "Neither heaven nor earth wept for them" (44:29). Egyptian funerary texts promise the dead king that "the sky weeps for thee, the earth trembles" (Pyramid Text Utterance 553)
findings.problem: Could not verify the utterance number or wording in Faulkner. The "Songs of Isis and Nephthys" quotation was also not verified. Also, 44:29 is a statement, not clearly an "inversion" of a formula.
findings.correction: Egyptian funerary texts speak of heaven and earth mourning for the dead (verify Pyramid Text utterance number against Faulkner before quoting)

findings.snippet: In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it ", a creator claim with no Egyptian parallel.
findings.problem: Egyptian royal ideology did claim the king's control over the Nile's inundation and kings were hymned as creators; "no Egyptian parallel" is unsupported.
findings.correction: In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it", a creator claim.

findings.snippet: The Bible has 600,000 men, about two million people, leaving Egypt, which archaeology cannot find any trace of.
findings.problem: The mainstream view is that there is no archaeological evidence for an exodus of that size. But the Quran gives no number, and its "small band" (26:54) is Pharaoh's description of the Israelites, not a claim about the real number.
findings.correction: The Bible has 600,000 men leaving Egypt, a number archaeology has found no trace of. The Quran gives no number but quotes Pharaoh describing them as a "small band".

findings.snippet: But Egyptian shemer means "foreigner/stranger" (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary II p.741), which fits a foreign agitator
findings.problem: Budge's Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary (1920) is outdated and this reading of the Samiri name is not supported by modern Egyptology; Egyptian lexica (Erman-Grapow, Wb) do not list this meaning. Other proposals: Hebrew shomer, Samaritan.
findings.correction: The Samiri's identity is debated; some proposals derive it from Hebrew shomer or from an Egyptian term (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary, a dated source).
sources: E. A. Wallis Budge, An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary (1920)

findings.snippet: the name is plausibly an Egyptian title (see Silverstein, JSAI 34)
findings.problem: Adam Silverstein's article "Haman's Transition from Jahiliyya to Islam" (JSAI 34, 2008, 285-308) argues the Quranic Haman has its origin in the biblical Haman of Esther, the opposite of the claim.
findings.correction: the name is argued by some to be an Egyptian title (Muhammad Asad, Hamen/Hmn), a view Silverstein rejects in JSAI 34, where he derives the Quranic Haman from the Book of Esther
sources: Silverstein, "Haman's Transition from Jahiliyya to Islam", JSAI 34 (2008) 285-308

findings.snippet: Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640) : names "the Arabs of Muhammad".
findings.problem: Thomas the Presbyter is dated to c. 640 and mentions "tayyaye d-Mhmt"; some scholars read Mhmt as a title, not a name. Doctrina Jacobi does not name Muhammad, only "a prophet"; P2 says all these name him.
findings.correction: Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640): mentions "the Arabs of Muhammad" (Mhmt, which some read as a title).
sources: Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It, pp. 116-117

findings.snippet: The Khuzistan Chronicle (c. 660) : the Arabs led by MHMD conquered Persia.
findings.problem: Could not confirm that the Khuzistan Chronicle names Muhammad as "MHMD"; check Greatrex & Lieu / Hoyland.
sources: Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It; Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier

findings.snippet: Chinese sources : the Tang dynasty's account and Du Huan (750s) describe the prayers, fasting, the ban on wine and the Friday sermon.
findings.problem: Du Huan's Jingxingji survives only in fragments quoted in the Tongdian; it does describe the Arab religion, but the claim that it names a "Friday sermon" etc. should be quoted from Hoyland's translation.
findings.correction: Chinese sources: the Tang account and Du Huan (750s) describe the Arab religion, including prayer and a ban on wine (check Hoyland for the exact items).
sources: Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It, ch. on Chinese sources

findings.snippet: The Arab-Sassanian coin of Bishapur/Kirman, 66-70 AH, reads "Muhammad is the messenger of God".
findings.problem: The Arab-Sasanian "Muhammad rasul Allah" coins are usually attributed to Bishapur (66 AH); the Kirman coin is later. Present as approximate.
findings.correction: The Arab-Sasanian coins of Bishapur (66 AH) and later issues read "Muhammad is the messenger of God" in Pahlavi.

findings.snippet: Sinai's verdict above is now the mainstream view
findings.problem: Sinai says Muhammad's prophethood as a late-7th-century invention is improbable; "mainstream" is a fair description but revisionist views have not disappeared. Stated more strongly than the source.
findings.correction: Sinai's verdict above is now widely held.

findings.snippet: Pre-Islamic Arab poets already knew a Dhul-Qarnayn (Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari )
findings.problem: The reports of Tubba' al-Himyari poetry about Dhul-Qarnayn are in Ibn Hisham and Ibn Hajar but disputed. Also does not answer the Alexander connection.

findings.snippet: The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated after 628, while Surah al-Kahf is Meccan (before 622)
findings.problem: The Syriac Alexander Legend (c. 629-636) is later than the surah on the Meccan dating, but it draws on earlier Alexander material, especially the homily of Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) which already has Alexander, the gate against Gog and Magog. The argument omits this earlier source.
findings.correction: The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated c. 629-636, but earlier material, including Jacob of Serugh's Alexander homily (d. 521), already links Alexander to the gate against Gog and Magog.
sources: Jacob of Serugh, Homily on Alexander

findings.snippet: Scholars such as François de Blois and Oliver Leaman warn that in the vast literature of late antiquity, parallels are "almost too easy to find"
findings.problem: Quote not located in de Blois or Leaman. Source unknown.
findings.correction: Scholars warn that parallels in late antique literature are easy to find and similarity does not prove influence.

findings.snippet: as Michael Pregill and Nicolai Sinai have noted
findings.problem: Could not confirm that Pregill and Sinai make this point about Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer specifically.

findings.snippet: Genesis Rabbah (38:13, 5th century, Palestine) has a version in which Abraham breaks the idols in his father's shop
findings.problem: Earlier Jewish texts have Abraham destroying idols: Jubilees 12 (2nd century BCE) has Abraham burn the house of idols, and the Apocalypse of Abraham 1-8 (1st century CE) has Terah's idols broken. Genesis Rabbah is not the earliest parallel; this undermines the point that sources are later.
findings.correction: Earlier Jewish texts already have Abraham attacking idols (Jubilees 12; Apocalypse of Abraham 1-8); Genesis Rabbah 38:13 (5th century) has the idols broken in his father's shop.

findings.snippet: Jesus and the apostles married (Peter, 1 Cor 9:5)
findings.problem: The New Testament never says Jesus married; 1 Cor 9:5 says Peter and other apostles had wives.
findings.correction: Peter and other apostles were married (1 Cor 9:5; Mark 1:30)

findings.snippet: Dirham here means a weight of silver ( Lisan al-'Arab : "a dirham of weight"), and payment in weighed silver is attested in Middle Kingdom Egypt.
findings.problem: The Arabic dirham derives from the Greek drachma, so the word itself post-dates Joseph; the answer shows the unit can mean weight but not that the term existed in his time. Silver by weight is attested in Egypt (deben), but Middle Kingdom evidence is thin.
findings.correction: "Dirham" in 12:20 can be read as a weight of silver (Lisan al-Arab), and silver by weight (the deben) was used in Egyptian payments; critics note that the word dirham comes from Greek drachma.

findings.snippet: impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt
findings.problem: Impalement of enemies is attested (Karnak inscription of Merneptah/Ramesses III); say "attested as a punishment" and avoid implying crucifixion.
findings.correction: impalement of enemies and criminals is attested in New Kingdom Egypt

findings.snippet: Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir
findings.problem: The Kattani classification (Nazm al-mutanathir) lists it as mutawatir; some scholars dispute and some modern writers read 54:1 as eschatological. Gradings by Hudhayfa and Ali chains are not in Bukhari or Muslim.
findings.correction: Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir (some scholars read 54:1 as eschatological)

findings.snippet: Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, Library of History 3.44) describes a temple in western Arabia "very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians"; Edward Gibbon read it as the Kaaba.
findings.problem: Diodorus places the temple among the Banizomenes on the coast, with uncertain location; Patricia Crone argued it is not Mecca. Gibbon accepted the identification with Mecca, but scholarly consensus is split. The page itself says "use with care".
findings.correction: Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 3.44) describes a very holy temple among the Banizomenes of western Arabia; Gibbon read it as the Kaaba, though others dispute the location.
sources: Crone, Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987)

findings.snippet: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which many scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca.
findings.problem: The identification of Macoraba with Mecca is disputed (Crone). The word could be South Arabian mikrab, "temple".
findings.correction: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which some scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca; others (such as Patricia Crone) doubt it.
sources: Crone, Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987)

findings.snippet: the Syriac Book of the Himyarites (a damaged 12th-century manuscript)
findings.problem: The only manuscript is damaged and was recovered from the binding of a codex bound in 1469; its date was not confirmed as 12th century. The text itself is 6th century.
findings.correction: the Syriac Book of the Himyarites (a damaged manuscript of a 6th-century text)
sources: Moberg, The Book of the Himyarites (1924)

findings.snippet: in the Greek Martyrdom of Arethas the persecutors ask them only to deny "the man called Jesus", not God
findings.problem: Could not verify this wording; other accounts (Letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham) record the demand "Deny Christ and the cross and become Jewish". Quoting it as "only" is unsupported.
sources: Letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham

findings.snippet: The prophecies below meet all four.
findings.problem: The prophecies in this section are drawn from hadith, which were transmitted orally and written down later; "recorded before the event" is not demonstrated for all of them (e.g., the Mongols, Hijaz fire).
findings.correction: Some of the prophecies below meet these four tests; others are weaker and should be used with care.

findings.snippet: Within a generation all three fell in that order (Musnad Ahmad).

findings.snippet: In the Septuagint text of Codex Sinaiticus, the original scribe wrote ΧΙΡΑ, which is how Greek renders "Hira". A later corrector changed it to ΧΕΙΡΑΣ ("hands").
findings.problem: The Septuagint of Isa 29:12 has "into the hands (cheiras) of a man who knows letters"; Greek scribes of Sinaiticus regularly spell ει as ι (itacism). ΧΙΡΑΣ is a spelling variant of χεῖρας "hands", not the name Hira, and the corrector's change is orthographic. The Septuagint also differs from the Hebrew ("knows letters"), so it is not the same reading.
findings.correction: In Codex Sinaiticus the word for "hands" in Isa 29:12 is spelled ΧΙΡΑΣ by the first hand (a common itacistic spelling of ΧΕΙΡΑΣ), which was later corrected; it is a spelling variant, not the name Hira.
sources: Milne & Skeat, Scribes and Correctors of the Codex Sinaiticus (1938)
Jongkind, Scribal Habits of Codex Sinaiticus (2007)

findings.problem: The Torah already required tithes and gleanings for the poor (Deut 14:28-29; Lev 19:9-10), Roman and Byzantine states had grain distributions, and the English Poor Law dates from 1601. "Where a 7th-century Arabian got it" ignores these precedents.
findings.correction: Modern states arrived at taxation-for-welfare in the 19th and 20th centuries, though earlier systems (the Torah's poor tithes, Roman grain doles, the English Poor Law of 1601) existed. Islam made it a fixed religious obligation in the 7th

findings.snippet: Isaiah walking naked. Isaiah 20:2-3 has God command Isaiah to walk "naked and barefoot" for three years. The Quran: "Allah does not command indecency" (7:28).
findings.problem: Quran 7:28 addresses the idolaters' circumambulating the Kaaba naked, not Isaiah; the pairing is the argument's own.
findings.correction: Isaiah walking naked. Isaiah 20:2-3 has God command Isaiah to walk "naked and barefoot" for three years, which Muslim writers contrast with the principle "Allah does not command indecency" (7:28, in a different context).

findings.snippet: The Arabic is a pointed play on the Hebrew: 'asinu (we will do) becomes 'asayna (we disobeyed)
findings.problem: Hebrew 'asinu is from 'asah ("to do"), while Arabic 'asayna is from 'asa ("to disobey"); they are different roots, so it is not a pun on the same word. "No one in Mecca could have constructed" is speculation.
findings.correction: The Arabic sami'na wa-'asayna sounds like the Hebrew shama'nu ve-'asinu, though the roots differ ('asah vs 'asa)

findings.snippet: It has no birth narrative of a divine Son and no atonement theology. This is the Jesus of the Quran.
findings.problem: Q presents Jesus as the Son of Man who will judge (Q 12:8-9) and contains high claims (Q 10:22), and its eschatological Jesus differs from the Quran's. "This is the Jesus of the Quran" is the argument's own comparison.
findings.correction: It has no birth narrative and no atonement theology, but it presents Jesus as the apocalyptic Son of Man, unlike the Quran.

findings.snippet: Even setting Q aside, Mark and James give the same picture of a Law-observant Jesus without a divine-Son theology.
findings.problem: Mark presents Jesus as Son of God (1:1, 15:39) and has the narrator declare all foods clean (7:19), so it does not give a Law-observant Jesus without a divine-Son theology.
findings.correction: Even setting Q aside, James gives a picture of a Law-observant community without divine-Son theology.

findings.snippet: Correcting Paul. In Acts 17:28 Paul quotes the pagan poet Aratus, "we are His offspring", a line originally about Zeus. The Quran: "He neither begets nor is begotten" (112:3).
findings.problem: Acts 17:28 does not claim a divine begetting, and 112:3 is not a reply to it; the "Correcting Paul" framing is the author's, not supported by the Quran.
findings.correction: Muslim writers contrast Paul's quotation of Aratus in Acts 17:28 ("we are His offspring") with the Quran's "He neither begets nor is begotten" (112:3).
